# Outdoor Station Power {.unnumbered}

On the desk, the station draws its power from a USB cable. In the garden, there is no socket (H2): the station lives on a battery, which a solar panel charges during the day. This chapter explains how this works, from what the station consumes to the battery monitor that reports its state with every measurement. The [design chapter](00-design.qmd) gives the list of the parts and how they connect.

The **solar panel** charges the **battery** through the **charger**; the charger powers the **Grove Shield**, the board that carries the XIAO; the **battery monitor** (INA219), on the + wire between the charger and the battery, measures what goes in and out. The **thermistor** is taped against the battery, but wired to the charger only. The [wiring](#wiring) shows each connection.

## What the station consumes

Everything starts from the consumption of the station: it sets the size of the battery and of the panel.

The [energy estimate](../Architecture/Phase-04/06-3-energy-and-review.qmd) of the current firmware gives an average current of **0.24 to 0.43 mA**, with the development board of the bench. The outdoor station adds a few permanent currents, taken from the datasheets of its parts:

| Part | Current while the station sleeps |
|------|----------------------------------|
| Grove Shield: its charger and its 3.3 V converter | about 35 µA |
| bq24074 charger, at night, without sun | about 4 µA |
| INA219, in power-down mode | about 6 µA |
| DS3231 clock module, without its LED (see [The DS3231 Module](../Appendix/04-ds3231-module.qmd)) | up to about 110 µA |

These add up to about 0.16 mA. On the other side, the XIAO sleeps with 14 µA, much less than the development board. All in all, the station should draw **about 0.3 to 0.6 mA on average, 7 to 14 mAh a day**. These figures are estimates from datasheets: the battery monitor gives the real behavior of the station once it is outdoors.

## The battery

A lithium battery stores the energy for the night and for the days without sun. The station uses a **lithium polymer (LiPo) battery**: a flat pouch of 52 × 35 × 6 mm, with a short cable and a JST-PH plug.

- **3.7 V nominal**: 4.2 V when full, about 3.0 V when empty;
- **1000 mAh**: with 14 mAh a day, it would hold **about two months without any sun** on paper. Winter reduces this: a lithium battery gives less of its capacity in the cold. The margin stays large;
- **protected**: a small circuit in the pouch disconnects the battery when its voltage falls too low, when it is overcharged, or on a short circuit. An empty lithium battery, discharged further, is damaged for good: the protection prevents it, even if everything else fails.

A LiPo pouch is not screwed: it is stuck to the bottom of the sealed box with double-sided tape. It must never be pierced, folded or squeezed, nor touch a sharp edge or a screw.

### Lithium and the cold

A lithium battery can **power** the station in the cold, down to about −20 °C, with less capacity. It must not be **charged** below 0 °C: in the cold, the lithium that comes back into the negative electrode during the charge deposits on its surface as metal, instead of going inside it. Each such charge loses a little capacity for good, and the deposits can end up short-circuiting the cell.

In winter, a sunny morning can follow a night of frost: the panel gives current while the battery is still below 0 °C. The charger must therefore know the temperature of the battery, and wait until it is above 0 °C (HN2).

## The solar panel

The panel turns light into current. It is described by two values, measured in full sun (1000 W per square metre):

- its **voltage**, 6 V: it must be higher than the voltage of the full battery, 4.2 V, with a margin, for the charger to work. The charger accepts 5 to 10 V, and Adafruit recommends 6 to 7 V panels for it;
- its **power**, 3 W: about 0.5 A at 6 V in full sun.

The station uses a generic panel of 145 × 145 mm, coated with resin for outdoor use, with a cable ending in a 5.5 × 2.1 mm plug, the plug of the charger.

The panel lies **flat on the roof** of the shelter. A flat panel receives less light than a panel facing south, tilted, mostly in winter, when the sun stays low: in December, about two to three times less. Even so, the margin is large. In December, in France, a horizontal surface receives on average roughly 0.6 kWh of sunlight per square metre per day in the north, and up to about 2 kWh in the south: the same energy as 0.6 to 2 hours of full sun. A 3 W panel then gives about 2 to 6 Wh a day. Even if half of it is lost, in the charger and on grey days, 1 Wh is about **250 mAh** at the voltage of the battery: more than fifteen times the 14 mAh the station needs.

## The charger

A lithium battery is never connected directly to a panel: the charger stands between them. The station uses the [Adafruit bq24074](https://learn.adafruit.com/adafruit-bq24074-universal-usb-dc-solar-charger-breakout), which does four things.

1. **It charges the battery safely**: first with a constant current, then, near 4.2 V, with a constant voltage while the current decreases, and it stops when the battery is full. A lithium battery charged above 4.2 V is damaged, and can catch fire.
2. **It powers the station while it charges** (*power path*): its **LOAD** output gives the station what it needs, from the panel when there is sun, from the battery otherwise. The station never stops when the sun comes or goes.
3. **It adapts to the panel**: when the light is weak, the panel cannot give much current, and its voltage drops if more is drawn. The charger then lowers its current, to keep the voltage of the panel up and to draw as much as the panel can give.
4. **It checks the temperature of the battery**, with a **thermistor**: a resistor whose value changes with the temperature, taped against the battery. With the thermistor named in its datasheet, a 10 kΩ NTC of the 103AT type, the bq24074 only charges between **0 °C and 50 °C**, with a hysteresis of 3 °C ([TI datasheet](https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/bq24074.pdf)). Outside this range, it suspends the charge, and the station keeps running on its battery.

The station uses a common 10 kΩ NTC, whose resistance changes a little faster with the temperature (its *B* constant is 4300, against about 3435 for the 103AT). The charger compares the same resistances, so the range moves: calculated from the B constant, it charges between about **+5 °C and +44 °C**, a few degrees more or less with the ±10 % tolerance of the thermistor. Starting the charge a few degrees above 0 °C is on the safe side for the battery.

### The charge current

The board of Adafruit charges with **1 A**: of its three jumpers 0.5A, 1.0A and 1.5A, the 1.0A one is closed when it is delivered. The maker of the battery gives no datasheet, and those of batteries of the same size and capacity disagree: 0.5 A at most for a [LiPol LP523450](https://www.farnell.com/datasheets/2026383.pdf), 1 A for a [Varta LPP 523450](https://novapart.co/datasheet/farnell:2531264/).

The panel settles it: the charger cannot give the battery more current than the panel gives, about 0.5 A in full sun, of which the station also takes its share. The battery never receives more than about 0.5 A, the more careful of the two values, and the jumpers stay as delivered.

The charger also has a **USB-C input**. From a USB charger, it would charge the battery at 1 A: the battery is charged by the panel only.

The thermistor is a small component with two legs. It has no electrical link with the battery: it is only taped against it, to take its temperature. Two wires bring it to the charger (see [Wiring](#wiring)). At night, without input, the charger draws about 4 µA from the battery.

Cheaper charger modules exist, built around the TP4056 or the CN3791. Their chip also has a temperature input, but on the modules sold, this input is connected to the ground, which disables it ([TP4056](https://wiki.adom.inc/ray/tp4056)): they would charge the battery in the frost. Enabling it means cutting a trace of the module and adding resistors.

## From the charger to the board

The LOAD output of the charger goes to the **battery input of the Grove Shield**, the board that carries the XIAO: two holes to solder, 2 mm apart, on the edge of the board next to its switch, which Seeed calls the *power bonding pad*. The Grove Shield has its own charger, made for a battery charged from the USB port, and a converter that gives the 3.3 V of the XIAO and of the modules. For the Grove Shield, the solar charger takes the place of its battery: its charger lets the current through to the converter. Together, they draw about 35 µA.

The charger of the Grove Shield cannot replace the bq24074: its input is made for the 5 V of a USB port and is protected by components that limit it to about 5 V, while the panel exceeds 8 V without load; and it has no thermistor input.

The power switch of the Grove Shield, which has two positions, connects the power bonding pad to the board. It is **ON outdoors**: in the OFF position, the board receives nothing from the solar charger. One rule follows: **the power switch of the Grove Shield is set to OFF before the USB cable is plugged in**, to program the XIAO. Otherwise, the charger of the Grove Shield would charge its "battery", which is the output of the solar charger.

## Wiring

![Power of the outdoor station](../../assets/diagrams/power_outdoor_station.svg)

The battery, the charger and the Grove Shield connect with **JST-PH connectors**, of two kinds:

- a **plug**, at the end of a cable, which goes into a socket: the plug of the battery, and the plugs of the JST-PH cables;
- a **socket**, fixed on a board, which receives a plug: the two sockets of the charger, BATT and LOAD, and the small socket supplied with each JST-PH cable.

Shops name them after their metal contacts: the plug, with holes, is the *female* connector; the socket, with pins, is the *male* connector. The power needs three of them besides the battery: two cables, and one socket. Each JST-PH cable bought comes with a socket: two cables give all three, and a spare socket.

- **Panel to charger**: the plug of the panel goes into the DC jack of the charger.
- **Charger to Grove Shield**: a JST-PH cable plugs into the LOAD socket of the charger; its two wires are soldered into the two holes of the power bonding pad of the Grove Shield, next to its switch, red to +, black to −. The board has no printed BAT+ and BAT−: the + and the − are checked on the board and on its [schematic](https://files.seeedstudio.com/wiki/Grove-Shield-for-Seeeduino-XIAO/res/Grove_Shield_for_Seeeduino_XIAO_v1.0_SCH.pdf) before soldering, since a reversed supply can damage it.
- **Charger to battery, through the INA219**: a second JST-PH cable plugs into the BATT socket of the charger. Its red wire goes into the VIN+ screw terminal of the INA219. The plug of the battery goes into the socket supplied with this cable, with two wires soldered to its pins: its + goes into the VIN− terminal of the INA219, its − into a **lever connector**, together with the black wire of the cable. A lever connector, such as the Wago 221, joins wires without solder: each bare wire end goes into a hole, and a lever closed over it holds it. The current of the battery goes through the INA219 on the + side, and the − of the battery goes straight back to the charger. The battery plug is never cut: two bare wires of a LiPo battery that touch can make it heat up, or catch fire.
- **Polarity of the battery**: the order of the + and the − in a JST-PH plug differs between battery makers. Before the battery is plugged for the first time, its red wire must arrive on the + marked next to the BATT socket of the charger; if not, the two wires soldered to the socket are swapped.
- **Thermistor**: the board of Adafruit connects its THERM pin to the ground through a fixed 10 kΩ resistor, which stands for a thermistor at 25 °C. A small copper track, the **THERM jumper**, marked THM, is cut to take it out of the circuit; then the thermistor is soldered between the THERM pin and the GND pin next to it, with two wires of 15 to 20 cm, and taped against the battery. [The THERM Jumper of the bq24074 Charger](../Appendix/05-bq24074-therm-jumper.qmd) explains why, and how to cut and check it.

The INA219 shares the ground of the station through its I2C cable: it measures the voltage of the battery against this ground.

## The battery monitor

The battery monitor is part of the station for good: at each wake-up, every 15 minutes, it measures the battery, and its values are sent with the weather measurements. A multimeter checks the battery and the panel by hand: see [Checking the Panel and the Battery with a Multimeter](../Appendix/07-multimeter-checks.qmd).

### What it measures

The **INA219** is a chip that measures a current and a voltage, read on the I2C bus. Its module carries a small resistor of 0.1 Ω, the *shunt*, through which the current flows. A current through a resistor creates a small voltage across it, 0.1 mV per mA here: the INA219 measures this voltage, and gives the current. It also measures the voltage on the side of the battery.

The INA219 is placed **between the charger and the battery**: all the current of the battery goes through its shunt. At each wake-up, it gives:

- the **voltage of the battery**, which tells its state of charge: about 4.2 V when full, 3.7 V half-way, 3.3 V close to empty;
- the **current of the battery**, with its direction: **positive** when the sun charges it, **negative** when the station draws from it.

### What it shows

On the dashboard, these two curves tell the story of the energy of the station:

- during the day, the **charging current** follows the sun: it shows whether the panel works, and when it gets dirty or covered with snow;
- at night, the **voltage** slowly decreases: its slope over the night shows the consumption of the station;
- over the weeks, the voltage at the end of the night shows whether the battery fills up again every day, or empties slowly, as can happen in December;
- a battery that ages loses its voltage faster at night than it used to.

The station can thus warn before it stops, instead of falling silent.

### Its limits

- It measures **at the moment it is read**, once every 15 minutes: a snapshot, not the energy that came in and out between two wake-ups. Counting this energy would need a *charge counter*, another chip, which stays awake all the time.
- When it is read, the station is awake: the current it measures is the current of the station **awake**, about 50 mA or more, not its sleep current.
- Its resolution is 0.1 mA, with a range of ±400 mA, which covers the panel and the awake station.

Between two measurements, the firmware puts it in power-down mode, where it draws about 6 µA according to its datasheet.

## Summary

| Part | Role |
|------|------|
| Solar panel, 6 V, 3 W | Turns the light into current, about 250 mAh a day in winter, at least |
| bq24074 charger | Charges the battery safely, powers the station, adapts to the panel |
| Thermistor NTC 10 kΩ | Stops the charge below about +5 °C |
| LiPo battery, 1000 mAh, protected | Holds the energy: two months without sun on paper |
| INA219 | Measures the voltage and the current of the battery at each wake-up |
| Grove Shield | Receives the power of the charger on its power bonding pad, and gives the 3.3 V |
